explanations.explanation: Zophar says it himself: "So my anxious thoughts compel me to answer, because of the turmoil within me." (Job 20:2) So he isn't claiming a message from above. He's saying the turmoil inside him is doing the pushing. I think we've all hit send while our stomach was still doing flips.

Zophar never says God told him to speak. He says his anxious thoughts compel him to answer, because of the turmoil within him (Job 20:2). That's a different thing from a word from God. The text leaves it at what's churning inside Zophar.

Job did cry out for pity just before this. But that's not what Zophar names as his reason for answering. He says, "So my anxious thoughts compel me to answer…" (Job 20:2). The push comes from the turmoil inside Zophar.

Yes, he says it right out: "I have heard a rebuke that insults me, and my understanding prompts a reply." (Job 20:3) Zophar took something Job said as an insult. I think that's why he's answering with both hands on the wheel.

It's true. Zophar says, "I have heard a rebuke that insults me, and my understanding prompts a reply." (Job 20:3) He says he heard a rebuke, and he says it insulted him. Then his understanding prompts him to answer.

explanations.answer: Since man was placed on the earth
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Zophar asks, "Do you not know that from antiquity, since man was placed on the earth…" (Job 20:4). He's reaching back to the very start of people on earth. When a man says it's been true since the beginning, he wants you to hush.
Zophar doesn't name Noah, or any person at all. He says "from antiquity, since man was placed on the earth…" (Job 20:4). That reaches back to when people were first placed on earth.

Zophar never mentions Babel. He says it goes back "from antiquity, since man was placed on the earth…" (Job 20:4). That's the start of people on earth, so he's claiming a much longer stretch than any one event.

Yes. Zophar says "the triumph of the wicked has been brief and the joy of the godless momentary." (Job 20:5) Brief and momentary, he says, and he says it's been that way the whole time. That's the point he's about to spend a whole speech on.
Zophar says the opposite. In his words, "the triumph of the wicked has been brief and the joy of the godless momentary." (Job 20:5) Endless triumph is exactly what he says doesn't happen.
Hidden isn't his word. Zophar says "the triumph of the wicked has been brief…" (Job 20:5). His point is about how short it lasts, not whether anyone can see it.
That's it. Zophar says "he will perish forever…" (Job 20:7). The head can touch the clouds, and he still says the man perishes. That's a long fall, and Zophar doesn't soften it.
Zophar says no such thing. Even with arrogance that reaches the heavens, he says the man "will perish forever…" (Job 20:7). Reigning isn't in the picture.
Thriving is the opposite of what Zophar claims. He says the man "will perish forever…" (Job 20:7). Head in the clouds or not, that's where he says it ends.
Right. Zophar says "those who had seen him will ask, 'Where is he?'" (Job 20:7) The people who used to see him around will be looking for him. Once you're gone, folks can only ask where you went.
It's true. Zophar says, "those who had seen him will ask, 'Where is he?'" (Job 20:7) The ones who used to see the man are the ones doing the asking.
Not quite. Zophar says the opposite: "The eye that saw him will see him no more, and his place will no longer behold him." (Job 20:9) The eye that saw him sees him no more. That's the whole line.
Yes, it's false. Zophar says, "The eye that saw him will see him no more…" (Job 20:9). No someday in there. He says the eye won't see him again.

explanations.answer: Seek the favor of the poor
explanations.explanation: That's what he says: "His sons will seek the favor of the poor, for his own hands must return his wealth." (Job 20:10) So the sons go to the poor, the very people the father is said to have wronged later in the speech. Zophar doesn't say how that goes.
Zophar doesn't mention a fight or any land. He says "His sons will seek the favor of the poor, for his own hands must return his wealth." (Job 20:10) The sons are the ones going to the poor.
A far country never comes up. Zophar says, "His sons will seek the favor of the poor…" (Job 20:10). They go toward the poor, not away from home.

explanations.answer: Lying with him in the dust
explanations.explanation: That's the line: "The youthful vigor that fills his bones will lie down with him in the dust." (Job 20:11) All that energy ends up lying down in the dust right along with him. I've seen what a long stretch in the dark does to a fella, and I'm glad I got dusted off.
Zophar doesn't hand the vigor to the sons. He says it "will lie down with him in the dust." (Job 20:11) The sons come up in the line before, and they're seeking the poor's favor there.
Neighbors aren't in this verse. Zophar says the youthful vigor "will lie down with him in the dust." (Job 20:11) That's where he says it ends up.

explanations.answer: His food sours into cobra venom
explanations.explanation: Yes. Zophar says, "yet in his stomach his food sours into the venom of cobras within him." (Job 20:14) It tasted sweet going in, and it turns the other way inside. That's a stomachache nobody wants.

explanations.answer: His food makes him strong again
explanations.explanation: Zophar says the reverse. "Yet in his stomach his food sours into the venom of cobras within him." (Job 20:14) Nothing in the verse makes him stronger.

explanations.answer: His food stays sweet inside him
explanations.explanation: The sweetness doesn't last. Zophar says, "yet in his stomach his food sours into the venom of cobras within him." (Job 20:14) Sweet in the mouth, venom in the stomach.

That's the word. Zophar says, "He swallows wealth but vomits it out; God will force it from his stomach." (Job 20:15) The wealth goes down and comes back up. And Zophar says it's God who forces it out.
Bread isn't in the verse. Zophar says, "He swallows wealth but vomits it out…" (Job 20:15). The thing swallowed is wealth, which is why the eating picture is about his riches.
No wine here. Zophar says, "He swallows wealth but vomits it out; God will force it from his stomach." (Job 20:15) It's his wealth that comes back up.
Not this time. Zophar says, "He will not enjoy the streams, the rivers flowing with honey and cream." (Job 20:17) He pictures rivers of honey and cream, and then says the man won't enjoy them.
Right, it's false. Zophar says, "He will not enjoy the streams, the rivers flowing with honey and cream." (Job 20:17) Rivers of honey and cream, and he doesn't get to enjoy them. Rough.

explanations.answer: He oppressed and forsook the poor
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Zophar gives: "For he has oppressed and forsaken the poor…" (Job 20:19). He says the man oppressed the poor and left them. I'll say it once, this is the heavy part of the speech.
Sacrifices aren't mentioned. Zophar's reason is, "For he has oppressed and forsaken the poor…" (Job 20:19). It's about how the man treated the poor.

explanations.answer: He gave his wealth to strangers
explanations.explanation: Zophar says nothing about giving to strangers. He says the man "has oppressed and forsaken the poor; he has seized houses he did not build." (Job 20:19) That's the reason he gives.
Yes. Zophar says, "he has seized houses he did not build." (Job 20:19) Houses somebody else built, and the man grabbed them. Zophar lists it right alongside oppressing and forsaking the poor.
It's true. Zophar says, "he has seized houses he did not build." (Job 20:19) That's one of the things he charges the wicked man with.

Right. Zophar says, "Because his appetite is never satisfied, he cannot escape with his treasure." (Job 20:20) Never satisfied is a tough way to live. It's like I always say about the cookie jar: there's no such thing as the last one.
Aging isn't in the verse. Zophar says, "Because his appetite is never satisfied…" (Job 20:20). The appetite doesn't fade. It never gets satisfied.
Zophar says the opposite. "His appetite is never satisfied," he says, "he cannot escape with his treasure." (Job 20:20) Never satisfied means never full.

Zophar says the opposite. "In the midst of his plenty, he will be distressed; the full force of misery will come upon him." (Job 20:22) Plenty doesn't bring peace in his picture. He says distress comes right in the middle of it.

Right. Zophar says, "In the midst of his plenty, he will be distressed; the full force of misery will come upon him." (Job 20:22) So he has plenty, and he still gets distress. No peace in that sentence.

That's what he says: "When he has filled his stomach, God will vent His fury upon him, raining it down on him as he eats." (Job 20:23) It comes right while he's eating. This is Zophar's claim about God, and the story isn't done with it.
It's true. Zophar says, "When he has filled his stomach, God will vent His fury upon him, raining it down on him as he eats." (Job 20:23) Both the full stomach and the fury are in the verse.
Yes. Zophar says, "Though he flees from an iron weapon, a bronze-tipped arrow will pierce him." (Job 20:24) He runs from one weapon and the next one finds him. It's a grim picture.
Zophar doesn't let him escape. He says, "Though he flees from an iron weapon, a bronze-tipped arrow will pierce him." (Job 20:24) The running doesn't save him.
The sons aren't in this verse. Zophar says, "Though he flees from an iron weapon, a bronze-tipped arrow will pierce him." (Job 20:24) Nobody comes to his rescue.

explanations.answer: What is left in his tent
explanations.explanation: That's right. Zophar says, "A fire unfanned will consume him and devour what is left in his tent." (Job 20:26) The fire takes the man, and then what's left in his tent. It's one more picture of everything going.
Neighbors' fields aren't in the verse. Zophar says the fire "will consume him and devour what is left in his tent." (Job 20:26) It stays at the man's own tent.
Gifts from the sons aren't mentioned. Zophar says the fire will "devour what is left in his tent." (Job 20:26) That's the answer in the verse.
That's the word. Zophar says, "The heavens will expose his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him." (Job 20:27) The sky shows his sin out in the open. Nowhere left to hide.
Zophar doesn't say forgive. He says, "The heavens will expose his iniquity…" (Job 20:27). Exposing is the opposite of covering over.
Forgetting isn't what Zophar says. "The heavens will expose his iniquity," he says (Job 20:27). The sin gets shown, not lost.

explanations.answer: The wicked man's portion from God
explanations.explanation: Yes. Zophar closes with, "This is the wicked man's portion from God, the inheritance God has appointed him." (Job 20:29) That's how he sums up the whole speech. It's what Zophar says, and the conversation keeps going.
Kings never come up. Zophar ends with, "This is the wicked man's portion from God, the inheritance God has appointed him." (Job 20:29) He's talking about the wicked man, not a king.
Zophar doesn't say every man. He says, "This is the wicked man's portion from God, the inheritance God has appointed him." (Job 20:29) He names it as the wicked man's portion.
